description: In Georgia, parents are liable up to $10,000 plus court costs for wilful or malicious acts of their children. Other legal theories may reach further.
shortAnswer: In the State of Georgia, parents are liable up to $10,000 plus court costs for wilful or malicious acts of their children which result in injury or property damage. O.C.G.A. Section 51-2-3. The same rule applies to non-parental guardians, and the child must be under 18 at the time of their bad conduct.

faq.q: Is there a way around Georgia's $10,000 limit on parental liability?
faq.a: O.C.G.A. Section 51-2-3 deals only with the "wilful" or "malicious" acts of minors. It does not cover situations where a parent negligently entrusts a child with a dangerous instrumentality and the child hurts someone. There may be a way around the $10,000 limitation in such scenarios.

faq.q: Can a parent be liable if their child gets hold of a gun and hurts someone?
faq.a: If a child is allowed to play with a firearm unsupervised and a negligent discharge occurs, and a parent permitted the child to get their hands on that firearm (either by giving it to them or by failing to adequately secure it), that parent may have legal liability.

faq.q: Are parents liable when their child crashes the family car or boat in Georgia?
faq.a: Under the "family purpose" doctrine, when a child is driving a car (or a boat) that is owned by their parents and negligently causes a collision, it may be possible to hold the parents liable (normally this means a claim under the parent's liability insurance). The doctrine applies to adult children also.

faq.q: What is negligent supervision by a parent?
faq.a: Parents have a duty to supervise their children. If a parent knows a child is behaving badly or has reason to expect their child to behave violently in a certain situation and fails to take reasonable steps to protect others, they may be liable.
